extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and using 'Watson' / gateway / fish-out-of-water characters to introduce readers to unfamiliar worlds, deliver exposition, and provide character arcs without alienating the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a Watson/gateway character to introduce the universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers need a character to whom some things must be explained. A Watson (aka The Howard, gateway character, the apprentice) lets readers 'ride along' and be introduced to the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for lowering the learning curve for readers unfamiliar with genre conventions; gives the audience someone to identify with who is getting oriented and figuring things out. Examples: Watson in Sherlock Holmes, Bilbo/Hobbits, middle grade portal fantasies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the gateway character an arc of growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Drop someone in over their head and watch them learn how to swim — the Watson/apprentice should change over the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An arc of growth keeps the Watson from being static or merely an exposition device and makes them interesting rather than annoying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'As you know, Bob' exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t use the Watson as a prop for telling the audience things the character should already know or information the audience already possesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: awkward dialogue that exists only to transfer information. Instead, reveal information via discovery, conflict, or scenes that justify why the character is learning it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the Watson retains agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your Watson has agency and is not reduced to a passive recipient of explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of agency makes the character grating over longer works; keep them capable in other ways or let them make decisions. Examples: portray Watson as competent but less brilliant than Holmes rather than idiotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have the Watson serve multiple functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements should do more than one thing; the Watson should not only be there for exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the character contribute to theme, plot, relationships, or emotional stakes in addition to orienting the reader, so they remain interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use buddy-pairing to equalize power dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pairing two 'fish out of water' characters (or pairing an expert and a newcomer where both have strengths) equalizes power and reduces annoyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buddy-cop dynamic (e.g., Jackie Chan/Chris Tucker) lets each character be expert in different domains and bounce off each other; this maintains agency and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force discovery rather than telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t give the Watson as much information as you planned; give them moments when they still don’t understand, then let them piece it together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates satisfying beats where the reader discovers along with the Watson rather than being spoon-fed exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective about what you make confusing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you intend to confuse readers, pick the confusing elements that matter rather than delivering a flood of unexplained details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too many simultaneous confusions leave readers ungrounded and likely to stop reading. Limit deliberate confusion to a few important mysteries or design states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground the reader before hitting them with confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide orientation and trust-building details first so readers feel anchored before introducing deliberately confusing elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounding can be achieved via reliable setting details, recurring motifs, or characters who can orient the audience; example: small throwaway lines (Buckaroo Banzai) that signal 'we'll explain later' and build trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signpost intentional confusion as a design state
rubrics_metrics.description: Align the reader’s confusion with the character’s confusion to show that it’s intentional and temporary — a designed narrative state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Watson is confused, the reader knows the confusion is by design and that answers will come; this makes puzzlement engaging rather than frustrating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stabilizing elements in chaotic scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting an avalanche of odd details, include stabilizing anchors (like recognizable factions or a secondary character) so readers can orient without understanding everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Thor: Ragnarok introduces Valkyrie and two factions which stabilizes the strange environment and makes continued engagement possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Watson to deliver targeted exposition and reinforce important concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Gateway characters are useful for introducing a concept and driving it home so it doesn’t get forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve this technique for concepts of particular import; use it to ensure the reader remembers key worldbuilding or plot elements rather than for every minor detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the Watson unbearably ignorant over a long work
rubrics_metrics.description: A Watson who constantly needs everything explained can become an 'audience favorite to hate' and drain a novel-length work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the character’s knowledge over time, give them competence in some areas, or evolve them so sustained ignorance doesn’t frustrate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and structure from other works to learn timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Study successful uses (e.g., Hitchhiker’s Guide, Dirk Gently, Buckaroo Banzai) to see when exposition is telegraphed and when to withhold explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze story outlines to see where explanations are needed and how they’re spaced; learn how to telegraph necessary exposition without overexplaining.
